description: Newtonian N-body simulation integrating the softened inverse-square law F ∝ 1/(r² + ε²)^(3/2) via kick-drift-kick leapfrog at 4 sub-steps per frame. The default configuration is a solar-system analogue — one heavy central body with four lighter planets on Keplerian circular orbits — chosen because it remains visually stable for well over 30 s. A 'Figure-8' button switches to the Chenciner–Montgomery choreography and a 'Randomize' button spawns 4–6 bodies with jittered ring positions and zeroed net momentum, producing a variety of near-stable dances. Each body leaves a 300-position fading trail that is the visual centerpiece; bodies are color-coded from warm amber (heaviest) to cool violet (lightest). The system resets to a new random configuration when any body escapes the canvas or after ~30 s.

title: Spirolateral Mandalas
tagline: 32 spirolateral figures drawn stroke by stroke — integer sequences turned into rotationally symmetric geometry via turtle graphics, cycling through two 4×4 gallery sets with a seamless crossfade
technique: canvas / spirolateral / integer sequence geometry / turtle graphics / rotational symmetry / requestAnimationFrame
description: A spirolateral is a turtle-geometry path determined by an integer sequence and a fixed turning angle: the turtle walks seq[0] units, turns right by A°, walks seq[1] units, turns, and repeats. The minimum number of passes R for the path to close satisfies R = 360 / gcd(360, n·A mod 360), connecting closure to number-theoretic divisibility. The piece shows 16 figures per gallery set (4×4 grid) drawn one stroke at a time via requestAnimationFrame, covering sequences ranging from [1,2,3] at 90° (classic square rosette) to [1,2,3,4,5,6] at 60° (hexagonal star) to Fibonacci-derived sequences. Each figure keeps one consistent color from a mint / rose / gold / violet palette on a deep navy ground. After all figures complete there is a brief pause, then a 0.9-second crossfade transitions to a second set with entirely different sequences and angles, looping seamlessly. Speed (Slow / Normal / Fast) and Skip controls are provided.

title: Smooth Life — The Creature That Has No Name
tagline: SmoothLife: a continuous-state, continuous-space generalization of Conway's Game of Life producing slow blobby organisms that drift and self-organize on a dark canvas in deep violet and electric cyan
technique: canvas / SmoothLife / continuous cellular automaton / logistic sigmoid / Float32Array / requestAnimationFrame
description: SmoothLife (Rafler 2011) generalizes Conway's Life to continuous state values in [0,1] and circular neighborhood kernels: for each cell, an inner disk average n and outer annulus average m are combined via logistic sigmoid birth/survival functions σ₂ — the same qualitative life/death rule as Conway's but infinitely smooth rather than threshold-hard. A 20×20 random seed placed at center self-organizes within ~50 frames into traveling blobs, rings, and branching filaments that fill the canvas. Two Float32Array buffers are swapped each frame; precomputed flat kernel arrays make the toroidal convolution efficient. Color maps 0 → near-black (#050508), 0.5 → deep violet (#7b3fff), 1.0 → bright cyan-white (#00e8d6), via a 256-entry LUT. The grid is rendered at 4× zoom with image-rendering:pixelated, giving the organism-under-microscope aesthetic.

title: Cloth: What Falls Together
tagline: 32×32 spring-mass cloth falls under gravity and sways in sinusoidal wind — Verlet integration with 5 constraint-projection iterations per frame, quads shaded by surface-normal depth in deep burgundy on near-black
technique: canvas / Verlet integration / spring-mass cloth / constraint projection / surface-normal shading / requestAnimationFrame
description: A 32×32 grid of particles simulates cloth via Verlet integration: each frame, velocity is computed as the difference between current and previous positions, gravity and a sinusoidal wind force are added, and five rounds of constraint projection keep structural (horizontal/vertical) and shear (diagonal) springs at their rest lengths. The top row is pinned at evenly spaced intervals; a sinusoidal wind force Fx = A·sin(t·ω + x·k) ripples the cloth continuously so it never settles to a static state. Each frame, 31×31 quads are drawn as filled paths shaded by the z-component of the surface normal (cross product of the two diagonals), giving a subtle sense of fabric depth: quads facing the viewer glow in deep burgundy (#8b1a3a), those twisting away darken toward near-black (#080810).

title: Hankin's Infinite Rose
tagline: 6-fold and 8-fold Islamic star tilings cross-fade and breathe — parametric star polygons in deep teal, warm gold, and off-white parchment on a near-black ground
technique: canvas / Islamic geometric art / star polygon / hexagonal tiling / square tiling / cross-fade / requestAnimationFrame
description: Two symmetry families of Islamic girih tilework cross-fade continuously: a hexagonal (6-fold) grid and a square (8-fold) grid, each with star polygons at every cell centre. Stars are drawn as regular 2n-vertex polygons alternating outer tips at radius R and inner notches at radius r. A hermite-eased sine wave over 960 frames morphs globalAlpha between the two layers, so neither family ever cuts abruptly. A secondary oscillation slowly varies the inner notch radius, making star points breathe from sharp to broad. The entire tiling rotates at 0.00025 rad/frame — one full revolution every ~70 minutes — so no fixed boundary is ever visible. Palette: near-black teal ground (#081818), deep teal tile fill (#0d4040), warm gold stars (#c8922a), and off-white parchment corner fills (#e8dfc0), referencing Persian and Moroccan zellige tilework.

title: Stadium Billiard: The Orbit That Never Closes
tagline: Square vs. Bunimovich stadium — 10 particles bounce elastically inside each table, trails colored by launch angle revealing ordered star patterns against space-filling ergodic chaos
technique: canvas / dynamical billiards / Bunimovich stadium / ergodic / integrable / elastic reflection
description: Two billiard tables drawn side by side: a square (integrable) and a Bunimovich stadium (chaotic). Ten particles per table launch from a shared seed point at evenly spaced angles, each coloured by launch angle using HSL 0–300°. Trails accumulate with low alpha so density builds over the 15-second cycle, after which all trails clear and a fresh cluster spawns from a new random seed. The square builds geometric star patterns because its motion is constrained to low-dimensional tori in phase space; the stadium fills space uniformly because curved caps mix the angle components, producing provably ergodic chaos.

title: Pursuit Curves — The Spider and the Fly
tagline: Six pursuit swarms (n=3–8) spiral inward simultaneously — each n-gon chases its neighbour, tracing rotationally symmetric logarithmic spirals in amber, teal, rose, lime, violet, and coral on near-black
technique: canvas / pursuit curves / logarithmic spiral / n-body pursuit / simultaneous update / trail fade / requestAnimationFrame
description: Six concurrent pursuit swarms — triangles through octagons — are superimposed at the canvas centre, each running the classic n-agent pursuit algorithm: every agent moves 1.5% of the distance toward its clockwise neighbour each frame. The simultaneous update preserves n-fold rotational symmetry, and the path of each agent is provably a logarithmic spiral. Distinct radii keep the six spiral families visually separated: the triangle (n=3) sweeps the outermost ring in amber while the octagon (n=8) traces tight coral spirals at the core. A 1.2%-opacity background fade creates a trail half-life of about 1 second, so roughly one full spiral cycle of accumulation is always visible. When a swarm converges to within 3 px of centre it respawns with its initial angle offset by π/n, depositing each new spiral between the previous one's traces and building a dense mandala over time.

title: SDF Kaleidoscope — Mirror Lattice
tagline: A WebGL sphere-tracer folds space with 48-fold octahedral mirror symmetry, blending spheres and rounded boxes through a pulsating smoothmin — neon crimson surfaces emerge from a near-black teal void as the camera slowly orbits the infinite lattice
technique: WebGL / SDF raymarching / kaleidoscopic IFS / octahedral domain fold / smoothmin / GLSL fragment shader
description: A fullscreen WebGL fragment shader fires one ray per pixel through a scene defined entirely by signed-distance functions. The domain fold applies abs() across all three axes then sorts the components, collapsing the infinite space into 48 mirror-equivalent octants before tiling with mod() — a kaleidoscopic IFS that is categorically different from plain translational repetition. Inside each tile, a sphere and a rounded box are blended via the polynomial smooth-minimum (smin) whose blend radius oscillates with a slow sin(time), continuously morphing the silhouette. Lighting uses single-direction Phong diffuse and specular, five-tap ambient occlusion, an electric-cyan rim light, and exponential depth fog into the near-black teal void. The palette — neon crimson surfaces on absolute darkness — contrasts sharply with the warm gold-on-indigo scheme of other raymarched pieces in this gallery.

title: Mondrian Recursion: The Rectangle That Cannot Stop
tagline: A canvas recursively subdivided by binary space partitioning assembles itself split-by-split in dusty rose, slate blue, ochre, off-white, and sage — then fades and starts over
technique: SVG / binary space partitioning / recursive subdivision / BFS animation / requestAnimationFrame
description: Binary space partitioning recursively divides an 800×800 SVG canvas: at each step a rectangle is split by a vertical or horizontal line at a ratio drawn from 0.5 ± 0.2, with the axis biased toward the longer dimension to avoid flat slivers. Splitting continues until a maximum depth of 6 or a minimum cell size of 40 px is reached, after which each leaf receives a colour from a five-colour palette (dusty rose, slate blue, ochre, off-white, sage green) chosen to differ from its sibling. The composition assembles itself breadth-first — largest rectangles first — at 80 ms per split so the viewer watches the structure emerge from coarse to fine. After the final leaf appears the piece holds for 4 seconds, then fades to off-white and redraws with a wholly new set of random splits. Thin near-black borders separate every cell, referencing the bold lines of Mondrian's rectangular compositions while the palette departs from his primary triad toward softer, more contemporary tones.

title: Differential Growth: Coral Maze
tagline: A closed curve crinkles into coral-like folds as edge-subdivision, short-range repulsion, and smoothing springs compete — 3 000 nodes of deep-teal bioluminescence on near-black, fading and restarting at 60 fps
technique: canvas / differential growth / spatial-hash repulsion / spring-mass curve / requestAnimationFrame
description: A closed curve of initially 16 nodes grows by inserting midpoints on any edge longer than 10 px. A short-range repulsion force (resolved in O(n) time via a flat spatial-hash grid) prevents nodes from overlapping, while a mild spring pulls each node toward the midpoint of its two neighbours for smoothness. Confined by a soft boundary circle of radius 360 px, the curve cannot expand freely and instead crinkles into dense, space-filling folds reminiscent of coral polyp edges, brain-coral furrows, and lettuce leaf ruffles — all surfaces where differential growth causes a boundary to grow faster than the area it encloses. The simulation runs until 3 000 nodes are reached, then fades to near-black over 80 frames and restarts from a fresh jittered polygon so no two cycles are identical. Palette: near-black teal ground (#050d14), translucent deep-teal fill, and a bright cyan-teal stroke (#00c8a0) that suggests deep-ocean bioluminescence.

title: Laminar Drift
tagline: 4 000 particles thread a time-animated sinusoidal flow field, coloring by heading angle through deep teal, gold, and warm white on dark charcoal — trails accumulate and decay without full canvas clears
technique: canvas / flow-field / sinusoidal noise / particle trails / requestAnimationFrame
description: 4 000 particles navigate a time-evolving angle field derived from three octaves of sin/cos sinusoidal noise — no external library, no simplex, no value-noise lookup table. The field is sampled at each particle's position scaled by 0.003, multiplied by 2π to obtain a heading, and the time parameter advances 0.0005 per frame so the flow shifts continuously without jump cuts. Particles wrap at all four canvas edges and respawn at a random position after ~300 frames, producing perpetual renewal that builds density without periodic resets. Each frame a low-alpha dark fill (rgba 0.03) dims old marks, creating trails that fade over roughly 100 frames. Color is mapped from the particle's current heading angle through a three-stop gradient — deep teal #0d7377 at angle 0, gold #d4a843 at π, warm white #fff5e6 at 2π — on a dark charcoal #1c1c1e ground. The piece shares the flow-field genre with 115 (simplex noise, periodic canvas clear, pen-plotter palette on cream) and 238 (curl noise, divergence-free velocity, speed-based color on deep purple), but diverges in noise construction, background, color scheme, and particle lifecycle.

title: Harmonograph: Where the Pendulums Rest
tagline: Two coupled pendulums decay across warm cream paper in deep indigo ink, tracing a spiralling Lissajous figure that fades to stillness and restarts from blank
technique: canvas / harmonograph / parametric decay / pen-plotter opacity / requestAnimationFrame
description: A four-oscillator harmonograph with frequency ratio 2.001:3 on x and 3:2 on y, all sharing a decay constant of 0.0025, run over t ∈ [0, 4000]. The irrational f1=2.001 prevents the figure from closing too early, spreading strokes across the canvas before the pendulums settle. 80 000 points are pre-computed; each animation frame draws 80 as a single canvas path segment, giving a visible stroke-by-stroke drawing effect. Stroke opacity is fixed at 0.6 — overlapping strokes darken naturally through translucency, producing pen-plotter density without explicit weight tracking. After the curve completes, a 60-frame fade returns the canvas to the paper color and the loop restarts from blank. Palette is strictly duotone: warm cream #f5f0e8 paper, deep indigo #1a1a2e ink. Piece 80 also uses harmonograph equations but cycles through five dark-background presets with variable stroke weight following the damping envelope; this piece uses a single carefully tuned parameter set with a light paper ground and flat opacity.

title: Sorted Light
tagline: A sinusoidal interference field is sorted column-by-column by brightness, dragging electric violet and amber gold upward in a gravity collapse that melts and reverses every cycle
technique: canvas / pixel-sorting / ImageData per-pixel / sinusoidal interference field / column sort / requestAnimationFrame
description: Three sinusoidal waves create a spatially varying interference field across an 800×800 canvas, mapping brightness to a three-stop palette: deep navy (#0a0a14), electric violet (#7c3aed), and amber gold (#fbbf24). A sort front sweeps left-to-right at 4 columns per frame, each column independently sorted descending by brightness — the canonical pixel-sort operation — dragging bright pixels to the top and dark ones to the bottom in a liquid-gravity collapse. The sorted state holds for 90 frames, then an unsort front sweeps through in the same direction, restoring columns to their original interference pattern; a second hold follows before the cycle repeats. Unlike the glitch-art piece (31), which simulates digital corruption via scanline displacement and chromatic aberration, this piece performs a deterministic brightness sort that reveals the latent structure of the wave field under an imaginary gravitational force.

title: Pendulum Wave
tagline: 20 pendulums with tuned lengths sync and desync in waves, braids, and spirals — pure physics producing complex interference patterns that fully realign every 60 seconds
technique: canvas / pendulum wave / simple harmonic motion / tuned-period coupling / requestAnimationFrame
description: Twenty pendulums hang side by side, each given a length so it completes exactly N full oscillations in 60 seconds, where N runs from 40 to 59. At t=0 all bobs are aligned at rest; within seconds the braid pattern unravels into travelling waves, figure-of-eight knots, and apparent spirals as the different periods drift in and out of phase. At precisely 60 seconds every pendulum is again at rest simultaneously, and the loop restarts seamlessly — no transition cut, no fade, just a consequence of the integer-ratio constraint. The bobs are colour-mapped along a cool-to-warm gradient from indigo through cyan to amber gold on a near-black background; strings are rendered at low opacity to keep visual weight on the bobs. All motion is computed in closed-form simple harmonic motion with no damping, so the loop is mathematically exact.

title: The Grain of Light
tagline: 8×8 Bayer matrix ordered dithering converts an animated four-wave plasma into a two-tone halftone that breathes and shifts — the structured-noise algorithm that gave 1980s computer graphics their grain
technique: canvas / Bayer ordered dithering / plasma / ImageData
description: An animated plasma field from four cosine waves — horizontal, vertical, diagonal, and radial — is thresholded each frame by the 8×8 Bayer ordered-dithering matrix, producing a two-tone halftone image that continuously breathes and morphs on a near-black ground with sand-gold grain. The Bayer matrix supplies spatially structured (not random) thresholds, so the resulting dots form diagonal stripes that self-organise into grid patterns at mid-densities, making visible the same structured discretisation that once gave early computer graphics their distinctive texture.

title: The Path Finds Itself
tagline: A recursive-backtracking DFS carves a perfect 40×40 maze cell by cell; a BFS wave then traces the single solution in gold — warm cream on deep charcoal, seamlessly looping at 60 fps
technique: canvas / recursive maze / DFS backtracking / BFS solving / requestAnimationFrame
description: An iterative depth-first search carves a perfect 40×40 maze cell by cell, with the DFS tip glowing terracotta against cream passages on deep charcoal; when carving completes a breadth-first wave fans out in amber until it reaches the bottom-right corner, then traces the single solution path back to the start in gold before fading to black and restarting with a fresh random maze.

title: The Labyrinth Writes Itself
tagline: Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion in the maze regime (F=0.029 K=0.057) runs entirely on the GPU via two WebGL2 ping-pong RGBA32F framebuffers — channels crystallise from five scattered seeds into a labyrinthine network at 60 fps, mapped through an earthy near-black to warm-parchment gradient
technique: WebGL2 / Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion / maze regime / RGBA32F ping-pong FBO / 9-point Laplacian / requestAnimationFrame
description: Two chemical species U and V self-organise on a 512×512 toroidal GPU grid via the Gray-Scott equations at F=0.029 and K=0.057, the maze regime where V forms a connected labyrinthine network of narrow corridors rather than the coral branches (pieces 17/96) or self-replicating spots (piece 180) produced by other parameter regimes. The simulation runs 20 GPU steps per display frame during warm-up so the full pattern emerges within seconds, then drops to 2 steps per frame at steady state. A three-stop palette maps V concentration from near-black channels through dark sienna to warm parchment walls, evoking carved stone illuminated from within.

title: The Loom Remembers
tagline: 60×60 threads interlace through four threading drafts — plain, twill, satin, and herringbone — warm terracotta warp meets cool indigo weft as the palette drifts over a 60-second cycle
technique: SVG / generative weave / threading draft / interlace clip masking / over-under rendering
description: A digital loom simulation where 60 warp threads and 60 weft threads interlace following four threading drafts — plain weave (1:1 alternation), 2/2 twill (diagonal rib), 4/1 satin (smooth warp-faced float), and herringbone (reversing twill V-pattern) — each cycling every 20 seconds. Each draft is encoded as a flat integer array read by a single warpOver(draft, r, c) function that indexes by (r % rows, c % size). Warm terracotta-to-cream warp threads run vertically, cool indigo-to-sky weft threads horizontally; a sinusoidal drift shifts both color gradients across the cloth over 60 seconds. A subtle highlight along the top and left edges of raised warp-over cells reinforces the three-dimensional over/under illusion on a near-black canvas.

title: Polarity — Magnetic Dipole Field Lines
tagline: Two magnetic dipoles animate on charcoal — 3 000 iron-filing segments align to the live B-field while optional RK4 streamlines trace the closed loops connecting north pole to south pole
technique: canvas / magnetic dipole / B-field superposition / iron-filing texture / RK4 streamlines / requestAnimationFrame
description: Two magnetic dipoles slowly rotate and drift, their combined B-field computed as a superposition of point-dipole fields B = (μ₀/4π)[3(m·r̂)r̂ − m]/r³ with a soft-core regularisation. 3,000 short iron-filing segments update orientation each frame to align with the local field direction, coloured from warm iron amber (#c8871a) at weak field to bright gold (#f5d060) near the poles where |B| is large. Optional RK4 streamlines trace closed loops connecting north to south pole, demonstrating ∇·B = 0 — every magnetic field line that exits a north pole must return to a south pole, forming the closed loops that distinguish magnetic fields from electric fields.

title: Event Horizon
tagline: WebGL fragment shader casts one ray per pixel onto a Keplerian accretion disk — Doppler blue-shifts the approaching side to cyan/white, red-shifts the receding side to crimson/amber, and bends rays near the Schwarzschild radius via first-order gravitational lensing
technique: WebGL / fragment shader / gravitational lensing / Doppler shift / FBM noise / fullscreen quad
description: A WebGL fragment shader fires one ray per pixel from a camera elevated 20° above the disk plane. Rays passing within ~2.5 Schwarzschild radii are deflected toward the disk plane by a first-order lensing approximation (deflection ∝ Rs / b²), reproducing the characteristic brightened photon ring around the shadow. The bent ray intersects the geometrically thin disk plane; if the hit radius falls between the ISCO (r ≈ 1.5 Rs) and the outer edge, emission is computed from a Shakura-Sunyaev radial temperature profile (T ∝ r⁻³/⁴) tinted by a relativistic Doppler factor that blue-shifts the approaching (left) half toward cyan and white and red-shifts the receding (right) half toward deep crimson and amber. FBM turbulence noise advected by orbital phase gives the plasma a swirling, filamentary texture that loops seamlessly at 60 fps. The event horizon is rendered as a pure-black circle; faint background stars show through the thin outer disk regions.

title: Celestial Veil
tagline: Three layered Perlin-noise emission fields drift and glow with additive canvas blending
technique: canvas / perlin noise / additive blending
description: Three independent Perlin-noise layers — ionized-hydrogen crimson, oxygen-III teal, and ultraviolet violet haze — are rendered into separate pixel buffers each frame and composited onto a black canvas with globalCompositeOperation “lighter”, so overlapping emission regions sum their colours as real nebular gas does. Slow per-layer drift at different velocities creates a parallax depth inside the luminous cloud.

title: Interference Star
tagline: A Maurer rose morphs between eight star-burst interference patterns — gold, cyan, and rose on deep navy
technique: canvas / Maurer rose / parametric / animation
description: A Maurer rose connects 360 evenly-stepped points on the rhodonea curve r = sin(n·θ), where each point advances θ by d degrees. The piece cycles through eight (n, d) pairs — (2,29), (5,97), (7,71), (3,113) and more — morphing continuously between forms by lerping both parameters so fractional values dissolve one interference geometry into another. Alpha-transparent strokes (opacity 0.15) accumulate during transitions to bloom luminous nodes at crossing points; the canvas hard-clears once the target is reached. Palette: #0a0a12 background with gold, cyan, and rose strokes on alternating forms.

title: Orbital Hymn
tagline: Real spherical harmonics Y_l^m displace a 40×40 sphere mesh — amber positive lobes and teal negative lobes morph through eight orbital forms on a deep indigo ground at 60 fps
technique: canvas 2D / spherical harmonics / associated Legendre polynomials / painter’s algorithm / parametric surface
description: Each vertex of a 40×40 latitude-longitude mesh is displaced radially by SCALE·|Y_l^m(θ,φ)|, where the real spherical harmonic is computed from the associated Legendre polynomial recurrence. Positive lobes glow in warm amber (#f5a030) and negative lobes in cool teal (#30d0c0) on a deep indigo (#1a0a3a) ground. The piece cycles through eight (l, m) pairs — mixing zonal (m=0), sectoral (|m|=l), and tesseral harmonics — with smoothstep-eased lerp transitions over 3 seconds. Faces are sorted back-to-front each frame (painter’s algorithm) with back-face culling and diffuse lighting from a fixed direction.

title: The Rhumb Lines
tagline: 16 loxodrome curves spiral pole-to-pole on a rotating wireframe globe — each path a constant compass bearing made visible in vivid colour
technique: canvas 2D / orthographic projection / loxodrome / Mercator parametrization / requestAnimationFrame
description: A loxodrome (rhumb line) crosses every meridian at the same compass bearing, spiralling toward the poles in a curve defined by the Mercator parametrization: lat(t) = 2·atan(eᵗ) − π/2, lon(t) = lon₀ + t·tan(β). Sixteen curves at bearings from 5.6° to 174.4° are converted to 3D Cartesian coordinates on a unit sphere, rotated around the Y axis, and projected orthographically onto a 700×700 canvas. Only the front hemisphere (rotated z ≥ 0) is drawn; segments crossing to the back hemisphere are clipped, producing the characteristic arc-and-disappear rhythm as the globe turns. A lat/lon wireframe grid at 15 % opacity in dim slate provides the cartographic reference frame. Curves are coloured by bearing angle via a full-spectrum HSL sweep.
